q: What is a pytest fixture?
o: A decorator that makes a test skip itself
A reusable function giving setup and teardown
A test that always passes by its own design
A flag to run the whole test suite in parallel
e:
Many tests need the same preparation: a test user, a database session, a temporary folder. A fixture is a function marked with `@pytest.fixture` that prepares it.
A test simply lists the fixture's name as a parameter and pytest passes in the result.
Code after `yield` is cleanup that runs after the test, even if it failed. `scope` controls reuse (per test, module or whole session).
r: Fixture = reusable setup injected by parameter name.
fa: A reusable function that provides setup (and teardown via `yield`) to tests that request it by parameter name

q: How many test cases does pytest run here?
e:
`parametrize` runs the same test function once for each set of values in the list. Three tuples → three separate test cases, each reported as passed or failed on its own.
This avoids copy-pasting nearly identical tests, and one failing input does not hide the others.
r: parametrize = same test, many inputs.

q: Which patch target makes this test intercept the HTTP call?
o: `patch("requests.get")`
`patch("app.services.get")`
`patch("requests.api.get")`
`patch("get")`
e:
`from requests import get` creates a NEW name `get` inside the module `app.services`, pointing to the function.
`patch("requests.get")` replaces the name inside the requests module, but `app.services.get` still points to the original function, so the real HTTP call happens.
Rule: patch the name where it is USED (looked up), not where it is defined.
r: Patch where the name is looked up.

q: An in-memory `UserRepository` that stores users in a dict and behaves like the real one is called a…
o: Mock
Stub
Fake
Spy
e:
These are all 'test doubles', stand-ins for real dependencies:
- Fake: a simple but WORKING implementation (in-memory repository, fake email sender that stores messages in a list).
- Stub: returns fixed answers ('always return this user').
- Mock: pre-programmed and later checked: 'was send() called once with these arguments?'.
- Spy: wraps a real object and records how it was called.
r: Fake = working lightweight version of the real thing.

q: How do you assert that code raises a `ValueError` in pytest?
o: `assert raises(ValueError)` placed after the call
`with pytest.raises(ValueError): parse('x')`
`try/except` followed by `assert True`
`@pytest.mark.error` above the test
e:
The test passes only if the code inside the `with` block raises ValueError; if no error happens, the test fails.
You can also check the message: `pytest.raises(ValueError, match="invalid")`.
A hand-written try/except that does nothing when no error occurs would pass silently and hide bugs.
r: Expect an error → with pytest.raises(...).
fa: `with pytest.raises(ValueError): parse("x")`

q: Which is a common root cause of flaky tests?
o: Using too many assertions in one single test
Depending on time, shared state or real network
Using fixtures to prepare the data for tests
Running the tests on a local developer machine
e:
A flaky test sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any code change. Teams then stop trusting the test suite.
Typical causes: depending on the current time, random values, test order, data left by other tests, real network calls, or `sleep()` used to wait for something.
Fix the cause (inject the clock, seed randomness, isolate data, mock the network, wait for conditions). Automatic retries only hide it.
r: Flaky = non-deterministic. Remove the source of randomness.
fa: Dependence on time, ordering, shared state, randomness or real network calls

q: Your project has 100% line coverage. What can you conclude?
o: There are no bugs left anywhere in the code
Every line ran, but edge cases may be unchecked
Mutation testing is no longer needed at all
The tests run fast on every machine and in CI
e:
Coverage measures which lines were EXECUTED during tests, not whether the results were checked. A test with no assertions still produces coverage.
It also misses combinations: a line can run while one important branch or input never gets tested.
Coverage is good for finding untested code, not for proving correctness.
r: Coverage shows what ran, not what was verified.
fa: Every line ran during tests, but not that the behavior was checked or that all branches and edge cases were covered

q: How do you reliably test code that depends on the current time?
o: Run the test only at one specific hour of day
Inject a clock, or freeze time with freezegun
Add `time.sleep` calls inside of the test body
Skip those tests when they depend on the clock
e:
Code that calls `datetime.now()` inside gives different results each time it runs, so tests can't predict it (and may fail at midnight or month-end).
Pass the time source in as a parameter, e.g. `is_expired(token, now)`, so tests give a fixed date. Or freeze time for the test with freezegun.
The same idea applies to random numbers and IDs.
r: Time is a dependency: inject or freeze it.
fa: Inject a clock (or `now` function) as a dependency, or freeze time with a library like freezegun / time-machine

q: Best practice for integration tests that need PostgreSQL?
o: Mock the whole ORM and assert on the calls made
Run real Postgres in a container, roll back per test
Use SQLite instead, since all SQL is standard
Point the tests at the shared production database
e:
Integration tests check that your code really works with the real dependency. Mocking the ORM tests nothing real; SQLite behaves differently from Postgres (types, constraints, JSON, locking).
Start a throwaway Postgres in Docker for the tests. Keep tests independent by rolling back each test's transaction or recreating the schema.
Never touch production data in tests.
r: Integration tests: real database in a container, isolated per test.
fa: Use a real Postgres (e.g. in a container via testcontainers or docker compose) and isolate each test with a transaction rollback or fresh schema

q: What problem does consumer-driven contract testing (e.g. Pact) solve?
o: It runs load tests against the deployed service
It checks providers still meet their consumers' needs
It compares UI screenshots to find the changes
It tests the database migrations of a service
e:
Service A (consumer) calls service B (provider). If B renames a field, A breaks, and maybe nobody notices until production.
With contract tests, A records exactly which requests it sends and which response fields it needs (the contract). B's CI verifies that it still satisfies every consumer's contract.
It catches breaking API changes early without a full environment of all services.
r: Contract tests = provider checks it still meets consumers' expectations.
fa: Verifying that a provider API still satisfies what its consumers expect, without running full end-to-end environments

q: What does property-based testing (e.g. Hypothesis) do?
o: It tests only the properties of each object
It generates random inputs to check invariants
It measures how much code coverage tests have
It records HTTP traffic in order to replay it
e:
Instead of writing examples one by one, you describe a rule that must ALWAYS be true, and the library tries hundreds of generated inputs, including nasty ones (empty, huge, unicode, negative).
Example rule: sorting twice gives the same result as sorting once, and keeps the same length.
When it finds a failure, it shrinks it to the smallest input that still fails, which makes debugging easy.
r: Property-based = test rules on many generated inputs.
fa: Generates many random inputs to check that invariants always hold, and shrinks failures to a minimal example

q: Mutation testing measures…
o: The execution speed of the code under test
Test quality: it plants bugs and expects failures
The memory usage of the code during a run
How often the code changes in the repository
e:
The tool makes small changes to your code, for example `>` into `>=` or `+` into `-`, and runs your tests for each change.
If the tests still pass with the bug in place, that mutant 'survived', meaning your tests do not really check that behavior.
It is slow, so it is typically run on important modules. Tools: mutmut (Python), Stryker (JS).
r: Mutation testing = do my tests catch deliberately planted bugs?
fa: How good your tests are: it injects small bugs (mutants) into the code and checks whether tests fail

q: What is the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern?
o: A deployment process for the releases of a team
Setup, one action, then assertions on the result
A mocking library that is used for Python tests
An Agile ceremony that teams hold every sprint
e:
A clear test has three parts:
- Arrange: prepare data and objects.
- Act: do the ONE thing being tested.
- Assert: check the result.
One behavior per test, with a descriptive name like `test_withdraw_more_than_balance_raises`, makes failures easy to understand.
ec:
def test_withdraw_reduces_balance():
    account = Account(balance=100)      # Arrange
    account.withdraw(30)                # Act
    assert account.balance == 70        # Assert
r: Arrange → Act → Assert.
fa: Structure each test as setup, a single action under test, then assertions on the outcome

q: What is `conftest.py` for in pytest?
o: Configuring the linters of the whole project
Sharing fixtures and hooks with the tests below it
Storing the test data files of the project
Defining the CI pipelines of the repository
e:
Fixtures defined in a `conftest.py` file are automatically available to every test in the same folder and its subfolders. You don't import them.
Typical content: database fixtures, a test client for your app, shared fake objects.
General pytest settings go in `pyproject.toml` or `pytest.ini`.
r: conftest.py = shared fixtures for a folder of tests.
fa: Sharing fixtures and hooks with all tests in that directory and below, without importing them

q: You are fixing a production bug. What is the recommended first step in code?
o: Fix it directly in the code and deploy it
Write a failing test that reproduces the bug
Add more logging only and wait for it to happen
Rewrite the whole module that has the bug
e:
A failing test proves you understood and reproduced the bug. When it turns green, you know the fix works.
The test then stays in the suite as a regression test: if anyone reintroduces the bug later, it fails immediately.
r: Bug fix = failing test first, then the fix.
fa: Write a test that reproduces the bug and fails, then fix it so the test passes

q: Why should tests not depend on execution order?
o: Test order is always alphabetical, so it is safe
Order can change; hidden dependencies cause failures
It makes the tests run slower than they should
pytest forbids tests that rely on any order
e:
If test B only passes because test A created some data first, then B fails when run alone, in parallel or in a different order.
Each test should create what it needs and clean up after itself.
Plugins like pytest-randomly shuffle the order to reveal hidden dependencies; pytest-xdist runs tests in parallel.
r: Every test must work alone, in any order.
fa: Order can change (parallel runs, random ordering, running one test alone); hidden dependencies cause failures that are hard to reproduce

q: Which assertion verifies that a mock was called exactly once with specific arguments?
o: `assert mock.called is True and mock.count == 1`
`mock.assert_called_once_with(42, retry=True)`
`assert mock(42, retry=True) is not None`
`mock.verify(42, retry=True, times=1)`
e:
`unittest.mock` objects record every call made to them. `assert_called_once_with(...)` fails if the mock was called zero times, more than once, or with different arguments.
Other useful ones: `assert_called_with` (last call), `assert_not_called()`, and `mock.call_args_list` to inspect every call.
r: Check how a mock was called with assert_called_once_with.

q: What does `patch(..., autospec=True)` add?
o: Faster mocks, since they skip the real object
The mock uses the real signature, so bad calls fail
Automatic assertions on every call that is made
Real network calls for the patched dependency
e:
A plain Mock accepts any method name and any arguments. If the real function's signature changes, your tests keep passing while production breaks.
With `autospec=True`, the mock copies the real object's methods and parameters, so a call that would be invalid on the real thing also fails in the test.
r: autospec = mocks that respect the real signature.
fa: The mock copies the real object's signature, so calls with wrong arguments or nonexistent methods fail

q: How do you test a FastAPI endpoint without calling the real database?
o: You cannot do it without starting a real database
`TestClient` plus `dependency_overrides[get_db]` fake
Patch `fastapi.FastAPI` itself in the test setup
Run the server and call it with curl in the tests
e:
`TestClient` sends requests to your app in memory, without starting a real server.
Because FastAPI uses dependency injection, you can swap any dependency for the test: `app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = lambda: fake_db`.
Remember to clear the overrides after each test (a fixture is a good place).
ec:
client = TestClient(app)
app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = lambda: FakeDB()

def test_read_user():
    r = client.get("/users/1")
    assert r.status_code == 200
r: FastAPI tests: TestClient + dependency_overrides.
fa: Use `TestClient(app)` and replace the DB dependency with `app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = fake_db`

q: What is the purpose of a load test with a tool like Locust or k6?
o: To find syntax errors in the source code files
To measure throughput, latency and errors under load
To check the code style of the whole project
To test the layout of the user interface pages
e:
A load test simulates many users at once to see how the system behaves: how many requests per second it handles, how slow responses get, and when errors start.
Look at p95/p99 latency (the slowest requests), not only the average, and watch CPU, database and connection pools to find the bottleneck.
Run it against a production-like environment.
r: Load test = how does it behave with many users?
fa: Measure throughput, latency percentiles and error rates under expected and peak traffic, and find the breaking point

q: What are smoke tests?
o: Tests that are run for fire alarms in buildings
A small, fast set of checks of critical paths
Exhaustive regression suites that cover everything
Security scans that look for known vulnerabilities
e:
The name comes from hardware: switch it on and check that no smoke comes out.
After a deploy, a few quick checks confirm the basics: the health endpoint answers, users can log in, one key page loads and one key action works.
If a smoke test fails, roll back immediately.
r: Smoke test = quick 'is it basically alive?' check.
fa: A small, fast set of checks that the most critical paths work, often run right after a deploy

q: How do you decide what to test and how much?
a:
- Test behavior and contracts, not internal details.
- Prioritize by risk: business-critical logic, money, security, complex branching, places that had bugs before.
- Pyramid: many unit tests for pure logic, integration tests at boundaries (database, APIs), a few end-to-end tests for critical user journeys.
- Edge cases: empty, null, limits, duplicates, concurrency, failing dependencies.
- Keep tests fast and deterministic so people actually run them.
- Use coverage to find gaps, not as a goal in itself.

q: How would you test code that calls an external payment API?
a:
- Hide the provider behind your own interface (`PaymentGateway`) and inject it.
- Unit tests: use a fake or mock of your interface; cover success, card declined, timeout, duplicate request.
- Adapter tests: stub HTTP with `responses`/`respx` or recorded responses; check the request format and how errors are mapped.
- A few integration tests against the provider's sandbox/test mode (often nightly).
- Test idempotency keys and webhook signature checks.
- Never call the real production API from tests.

q: Unit test vs integration test?
o: They are the same thing under two different names
Unit: one piece alone. Integration: parts together
Integration tests are always done manually by hand
Unit tests always need a running server to work
e:
Unit test: tiny and fast (milliseconds). Tests one function with its dependencies replaced by fakes. When it fails, you know exactly where.
Integration test: checks that real parts fit together: your repository with a real PostgreSQL, or your API with its middleware. Slower but catches problems unit tests can't.
End-to-end tests go further and test the whole system like a user.
r: Unit = one piece alone. Integration = pieces together.
fa: A unit test checks one small piece (a function or class) in isolation; an integration test checks several parts working together, e.g. code + real database

q: How does pytest find tests by default?
o: It runs every Python file in the project folder
Files `test_*.py`, functions `test_*`, classes `Test*`
Only files in a folder that is named pytest
You must register each test by hand in a file
e:
Run `pytest` in your project and it searches the folders for files named `test_something.py`, then runs every function whose name starts with `test_`.
If you name a function `check_login()`, pytest will silently ignore it.
Useful options: `pytest -k login` (only matching names), `pytest -x` (stop at first failure), `pytest -v` (verbose).
r: pytest runs test_*.py files and test_* functions.
fa: Files named `test_*.py` or `*_test.py`, functions starting with `test_`, and classes starting with `Test`

q: What happens when an `assert` statement in a pytest test is false?
o: Nothing happens and the test continues to run
The test fails, and pytest shows the compared values
Python crashes with a traceback and stops all tests
The test is skipped and flagged in the report
e:
`assert condition` raises an AssertionError when the condition is false. pytest catches it, marks the test as FAILED and shows a detailed message, e.g. `assert 25 == 30`, so you see what the code actually returned.
If the condition is true, nothing happens and the test passes.
r: assert false → test fails with the compared values shown.
fa: The test fails, and pytest shows the values that were compared

q: In testing, what is a mock?
o: A failing test that is written before the code
A fake object that stands in for a real dependency
A copy of the production environment for testing
A very slow test that runs once in a while
e:
Real dependencies can be slow, cost money, or be unpredictable (sending an email, charging a card, calling an API).
A mock stands in for them during a test: you decide what it returns, and afterwards you can check how your code called it, e.g. 'was send_email called once with this address?'.
In Python: `unittest.mock.Mock` and `patch`.
r: Mock = stand-in that you control and inspect.
fa: A fake object that replaces a real dependency (like an API client) and records how it was used

q: What is the main benefit of an automated test suite?
o: It makes the application run faster in production
It catches regressions in minutes, before users do
It replaces the need for code reviews entirely
It writes the documentation automatically for you
e:
Without tests, every change risks breaking something elsewhere, and you only find out in production.
With a good test suite, CI runs all tests on every change; a broken behavior fails a test right away. That makes refactoring and adding features much safer and faster.
Tests also document how code is supposed to behave.
r: Tests = safety net against regressions.
fa: It catches regressions: when a change breaks something that used to work, you find out in minutes, not from users

q: What does test coverage measure?
o: How many tests exist in the project in total
The share of lines or branches run by the tests
How fast the tests of the suite finally run
How many bugs exist in the code of the project
e:
A coverage tool (e.g. `pytest --cov`) watches which lines run during the tests and reports a percentage, plus which lines were never executed.
Those uncovered lines are code no test checks at all, good places to add tests.
High coverage does not guarantee good tests: it doesn't check that assertions are meaningful.
r: Coverage = % of code executed by tests.
fa: The percentage of code lines (or branches) executed while the tests run

q: Which is an edge case for a function that returns the average of a list?
o: A list with 3 normal numbers
An empty list (division by zero)
A list of positive integers
A list sorted ascending
e:
Edge cases are unusual or extreme inputs at the boundaries, where bugs like to hide: empty input, one element, zero, negative numbers, very large values, duplicates, None.
An average divides by the length; with an empty list that is division by zero. Decide what should happen (return None? raise ValueError?) and test it.
r: Always test empty, one, zero, negative, huge, None.

q: Which describes a good unit test?
o: Slow but thorough, and depends on the internet
Fast, isolated from others, and deterministic
Tests many unrelated behaviors at the same time
Only runs on the CI server and never locally
e:
Good unit tests run in milliseconds (so you run them constantly), don't depend on other tests or on the network/database (isolated), and always give the same result (deterministic).
Each test checks one behavior and has a name that explains it. If a test is slow or random, people stop trusting and running it.
r: Good unit test = fast, isolated, deterministic.
fa: Fast, isolated from other tests and external systems, and deterministic (same result every run)

q: What is Selenium WebDriver?
o: A library that drives a real browser from code
A database in which test results are stored
A CSS framework that is used to style reports
A Java build tool that compiles and runs tests
e:
Selenium automates browsers. Your test code (Java, Python, JS...) sends commands to a driver (ChromeDriver, GeckoDriver), which controls a real browser: open a URL, find elements, click, type, and check the text on screen.
Used for end-to-end (E2E) UI tests that check complete user flows (login, checkout).
Selenium Manager (built in since 4.6) downloads the right driver automatically.
r: Selenium = code that drives a real browser.
fa: A library that controls a real web browser (click, type, read) from code to automate UI tests, using drivers such as ChromeDriver

q: Which locator strategy is generally the most robust in Selenium?
o: A stable attribute such as `id` or `data-testid`
Absolute XPath like `/html/body/div[3]/div[2]/button`
The position number of the element
The text color of the element
e:
Locators find elements: `By.id`, `By.name`, `By.cssSelector`, `By.xpath`, `By.linkText`.
A locator breaks when the page changes. Absolute XPath breaks with any layout change. Stable hooks are best: `id` or a test attribute like `data-testid="submit"`, agreed with the front-end team.
CSS selectors are usually faster and more readable than XPath; use XPath when you need text or parent navigation.
r: Prefer id / data-testid. Avoid long absolute XPath.
fa: A dedicated, stable attribute such as `id` or `data-testid`; avoid long absolute XPath tied to page layout

q: Why is `Thread.sleep(5000)` a bad way to wait in UI tests, and what is better?
o: It always waits fully; use explicit waits instead
It crashes the browser when the time is long
Selenium forbids it in all of its drivers
It is the best approach for slow web pages
e:
Pages load asynchronously, so tests must wait for elements. A fixed sleep is either too long (slows the suite) or too short (random failures).
Explicit wait: `new WebDriverWait(driver, Duration.ofSeconds(10)).until(ExpectedConditions.visibilityOfElementLocated(...))` polls until the condition is true or times out.
Implicit waits apply globally to element lookups; do not mix implicit and explicit waits, since the total time becomes unpredictable.
r: Wait for a condition, not for a fixed time.
fa: It always waits the full time (slow) and can still be too short (flaky); use explicit waits (`WebDriverWait` with expected conditions) that continue as soon as the condition is true

q: What is the Page Object Model (POM)?
o: Each page is a class with locators and actions
A way to store photos that tests will compare
A Maven plugin that builds the pages of the app
A database schema that describes the pages
e:
Without POM, locators are scattered across tests; when a button's id changes you edit dozens of tests.
With POM, `LoginPage` has methods like `loginAs(user, pass)`; tests call them and never mention locators. If the UI changes, you fix the page class once.
Tests become readable: `loginPage.loginAs("ana", "secret"); assertTrue(dashboard.isVisible());`
r: POM = one class per page; locators live there, not in tests.
fa: A design pattern where each page (or component) is a class holding its locators and actions, so tests read like user steps and a UI change is fixed in one place

q: What does `StaleElementReferenceException` mean?
o: The element was re-rendered; find it again
The browser is out of date and needs an update
The driver executable is missing from the system
The element is hidden behind another element
e:
Selenium keeps a reference to a DOM element. If the page re-renders (React updates, AJAX refresh, navigation), the old element is replaced by a new one even if it looks identical, and the old reference becomes stale.
Fix: re-locate the element right before using it, do not store `WebElement` objects for long, and wait for the page to settle (explicit waits). Page objects that look up elements on each action avoid this.
r: Stale = the DOM element was replaced; locate it again.
fa: The element you found earlier was removed or re-rendered in the DOM, so the stored reference is no longer valid; find it again (and wait properly)

q: What is Selenium Grid used for?
o: Running tests in parallel across many machines
Drawing tables of results for the test reports
Managing the databases that tests rely upon
Compiling the Java code of the test project
e:
One machine running tests one by one makes a big UI suite slow. Selenium Grid has a hub/router and several nodes; tests ask for a browser (Chrome 120 on Linux) and the Grid sends them to a free node, running many in parallel.
Typically deployed with Docker or Kubernetes, or replaced by cloud services (BrowserStack, Sauce Labs).
Parallel tests must be independent: separate data, no shared state.
r: Grid = parallel, cross-browser execution.
fa: Running tests in parallel across many browsers, versions and machines (or containers)

q: Which JUnit 5 annotations run before each test and mark a parameterized test?
o: `@BeforeEach` and `@ParameterizedTest`
`@SetupAll` and `@LoopTest` annotations
`@InitEach` and `@ManyTimes` annotations
`@BeforeTest` and `@Params` annotations
e:
JUnit 5 (Jupiter) basics:
- `@Test`: a test method.
- `@BeforeEach` / `@AfterEach`: run around every test (set up and clean up).
- `@BeforeAll` / `@AfterAll`: once per class (static).
- `@ParameterizedTest` with `@ValueSource`, `@CsvSource`: run one test with many inputs.
- `@DisplayName`, `@Disabled`, `@Nested`.
Assertions: `assertEquals`, `assertTrue`, `assertThrows`. AssertJ offers fluent alternatives.
r: @BeforeEach = per test. @ParameterizedTest = many inputs.

q: Selenium, Playwright and Cypress: what is a fair comparison?
o: Selenium is mature; Playwright and Cypress auto-wait
They are identical in every feature that they have
Selenium is a database for storing test results
Cypress supports every programming language there is
e:
- Selenium WebDriver: oldest and most widespread, supports Java, Python, C#, JS and all major browsers; very common in enterprise Java shops; you handle waits yourself.
- Playwright (Microsoft): multi-browser, multi-language, built-in auto-waiting, tracing, fast.
- Cypress: JavaScript/TypeScript only, runs inside the browser, great debugging, more limited cross-tab and cross-browser support.
Selenium is still very common in Java teams, so know WebDriver, waits, locators and POM.
r: Selenium = standard and flexible; Playwright/Cypress = modern with auto-waiting.
fa: Selenium: mature, many languages and browsers, W3C standard; Playwright and Cypress: newer, with auto-waiting and developer-friendly tooling (Cypress runs in the browser, JS only)

q: Why should the UI test automation suite be small compared to unit tests?
o: UI tests are slow and brittle, so keep only a few
UI tests are free to maintain, so write many more
Unit tests cannot find real bugs in the logic
Browsers are very fast, so UI tests are cheap
e:
Test pyramid: many unit tests (fast, cheap), fewer integration tests, very few UI/E2E tests (slow, depend on browsers, network, data).
Use UI automation for the most important user journeys (login, purchase) and smoke tests after deployment.
Test business rules, validation and edge cases through unit or API tests.
r: Few UI tests, many unit tests.
fa: UI tests are slow, brittle and expensive to maintain, so keep a few critical end-to-end flows and test most logic at lower levels (the test pyramid)

q: How would you design a maintainable Selenium (Java) test automation framework?
a:
- Stack: Java, JUnit 5 (or TestNG), Selenium WebDriver, Maven, AssertJ, reporting (Allure).
- Structure: Page Object Model; small component classes for shared widgets; tests only describe user steps.
- Stability: stable locators (`data-testid`), explicit waits only, no `Thread.sleep`, retries only for known infrastructure noise.
- Data: create test data through the API or database before the test; independent tests that can run in any order and in parallel.
- Execution: headless Chrome in CI (GitHub Actions/Jenkins), Selenium Grid or Docker for parallel and cross-browser runs; screenshots and logs on failure.
- Scope: few E2E flows for critical journeys; the rest at unit and API level.

q: Why do developers write tests?
o: To check the code works as expected, early on
To make the program run faster in production
Because every compiler requires them to build
To increase the total file size of the program
e:
Without tests, every change might silently break something else and you only find out when users complain.
With tests, you run a command and see in seconds whether the important behavior still works.
Tests also act as living documentation of how the code should behave.
r: Tests = a safety net for changes.
fa: To check that the code behaves as expected and to catch problems early, especially when the code changes later

q: Manual testing vs automated testing?
o: Manual: a person runs steps; automated: code does
Automated tests need no code to be written at all
Manual tests are always better than automated ones
They are the same thing under two different names
e:
Manual testing is good for exploring, judging usability and trying unexpected things.
Automated tests are written once and run on every change (CI), so they are ideal for repeated checks like regression tests.
Tools: JUnit (Java), pytest (Python), Selenium (browser UI).
r: Manual = a human. Automated = code.
fa: Manual: a person performs the steps and checks the result; automated: code runs the checks quickly and repeatedly

q: What are a test case and a test suite?
o: A case checks one scenario; a suite groups cases
A test case is a computer case; a suite is a room
A suite is one single test; a case is many tests
Both of them are error messages shown in pytest
e:
Test case: 'when I log in with a wrong password, I should see an error message and not enter'. It has steps, input data and an expected result.
Test suite: a collection of test cases, for example 'all login tests' or 'all tests of the project'.
In code, one test method is usually one case, and a test class or folder is a suite.
r: Case = one scenario. Suite = a group of cases.
fa: A test case checks one scenario against an expected result; a suite is a group of test cases run together

q: What is regression testing?
o: Re-running tests to check old features still work
Testing only the new feature that was just added
Testing the database backup that was just made
Testing the speed of the app on old hardware
e:
A regression is when something that used to work breaks after a change.
Regression testing re-checks old behavior every time you change the code. It is the main reason to automate tests: running hundreds of old checks by hand every release is not realistic.
When you fix a bug, you add a test for it, which keeps that bug from coming back.
r: Regression test = did my change break something old?
fa: Re-running tests after a change to make sure existing features still work

q: What does QA stand for, and what does a QA engineer do?
o: Quality Assurance: ensures quality through testing
Quick Answer: replies to the customers by email
Query Application: writes the SQL for the apps
Quality Angle: designs the logos of the company
e:
QA engineers (or testers) design test cases, run manual and automated tests, report bugs clearly and check fixes.
Some focus on automation: writing frameworks with tools such as Selenium. Developers also test their own code, so quality is a team responsibility.
A good bug report has steps to reproduce, expected result, actual result, and environment.
r: QA = Quality Assurance.
fa: Quality Assurance: helps make sure the software meets quality expectations through testing, test automation and better processes

q: What is Selenium?
o: An umbrella project of tools to automate browsers
A database that stores the results of tests
A cloud provider that rents servers by the hour
A Java framework for building backend servers
e:
Selenium can open a real browser and do what a user does: click, type, read text.
Its parts: WebDriver (the core, a common interface for many browsers), Selenium IDE (records and plays back actions) and Selenium Grid (runs tests in parallel on many machines).
It supports Java, Python, C#, Ruby, JavaScript and Kotlin.
r: Selenium = automate browsers for UI tests.
fa: An umbrella project of tools and libraries for automating web browsers, mostly used to test web UIs

q: What are JUnit and pytest?
o: Testing frameworks for Java and Python respectively
Cloud services that run tests on remote servers
Databases that store the results of test runs
Build tools that compile and package the projects
e:
A testing framework gives you a standard way to write test methods, check results with assertions, set up data and see a report.
JUnit is the main one for Java (JUnit 5 introduced the Jupiter style; JUnit 6 is the newest major version and requires Java 17 or newer). pytest is the most popular for Python.
Build tools like Maven run them with `mvn test`.
r: JUnit = Java tests. pytest = Python tests.
fa: Testing frameworks: JUnit for Java and pytest for Python, used to write and run automated tests
